title: Rarest Coat Colors
short_description: One of the hardest quizzes, devoted to rare Champagne and Pearl dilutions, including pseudo-double-cream phenotypes. Designed for the most experienced coat-color enthusiasts.
intro: One of the hardest quizzes, devoted to rare Champagne and Pearl dilutions, including pseudo-double-cream phenotypes. Designed for the most experienced coat-color enthusiasts.
questionImagesAlt: Photo of a horse for identifying its coat color

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Gold champagne is the Champagne dilution on a chestnut base. The coat becomes an even golden-apricot or silky yellow shade, often with a distinctive metallic sheen, while the mane and tail are commonly diluted to straw or nearly white. It can therefore resemble palomino. Typical Champagne markers include pink skin that develops darker freckling, especially around the eyes and muzzle, and amber or hazel-green eyes; foals are usually born with blue eyes.

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Classic champagne is the Champagne dilution on a black base. The coat is diluted to an unusual brownish-gray, taupe, lilac-brown, olive, or coffee-with-milk shade, often with a metallic sheen. The mane and tail are usually somewhat darker than the body, tending toward dark brown or chocolate. As with other Champagne horses, the skin is pinkish and develops darker mottling or freckles with age, while the eyes mature from blue in foals to amber or hazel.

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Amber champagne is the Champagne dilution on a bay base. The body becomes warm golden-brown or amber, while the mane, tail, lower legs, and ear tips are diluted from black to chocolate or dark brown. The characteristic Champagne markers are pink skin that develops dark freckling around the eyes and muzzle and amber or hazel-green eyes, which are blue at birth.

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Chestnut pearl, often called apricot, results from homozygous Pearl (prl/prl) on a chestnut base. The coat becomes a soft warm apricot or peach shade, often with a deep pearly sheen, and the mane and tail are usually similar in color or slightly lighter. Typical features include pale pink to lilac-toned skin, sometimes developing sparse darker mottling with age, and amber or hazel eyes; foals may be born with blue eyes.

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Sable champagne is Champagne dilution on a seal-brown or very dark bay-type base. The body is typically muted brownish-gold, olive-tan, or dark coffee-with-milk, while the legs, ears, mane, and tail remain a deeper chocolate shade. Because it can resemble classic champagne, genetic testing may be needed for confident identification. Like other Champagne horses, it has pinkish skin that develops dark freckling with age and amber or hazel eyes that are blue in newborn foals.

questions.question: What coat color is this?
questions.explanation: Buckskin pearl is the compound Cream/Pearl genotype Cr/prl on a bay base. Because Cream and Pearl are alleles at the same SLC45A2 locus, this compound heterozygote produces a strong pseudo-double-cream dilution. The body becomes pale beige, milky caramel, or soft cream-gold, while the mane, tail, lower legs, and ear points remain darker brown or coffee-chocolate. Pink to pale lilac-gray skin and amber, greenish, or blue-toned eyes are typical.
